paragraphs: And it was in the same nervous frenzy that he spoke. Meeting Fyodor Pavlovitch in the drawing-room just as he came in, he shouted to him, waving his arms, “I’m going upstairs to my room, not in to you. Good-by!” and brushed past, trying not even to look at his father. It may well be that the old man was simply too hateful to him just then. But so blunt a show of hostility surprised even Fyodor Pavlovitch. The old man obviously wanted to tell him something right away and had come out to the drawing-room on purpose to meet him. Given this friendly greeting, he stood silent and, with an ironical look, watched his son go up the stairs until he was out of sight.
“What’s got into him?” he asked Smerdyakov at once; Smerdyakov had followed Ivan in.
“He’s angry about something. Who knows?” the valet muttered evasively.
“Damn him! Let him be angry, then. Bring in the samovar and be off with you. Quick about it! Any news?”

Then came a string of questions, the sort Smerdyakov had just been complaining about to Ivan, all concerning his expected visitor. We will leave these questions out. Half an hour later the house was locked up, and the crazy old man was wandering from room to room in feverish expectation of hearing the agreed five knocks at any moment. Now and then he peered out into the darkness, and saw nothing.

It was very late, but Ivan was still awake and thinking. He stayed up that night until two. We will not set down his thoughts, though; this is not the place to look into that soul—its turn will come. Even if one tried, it would be hard to report them, because there were no thoughts in his head, only something very vague and, above all, intense agitation. He felt himself that he had lost his bearings. All sorts of strange, almost startling desires fretted him, too. After midnight, for instance, he was gripped by an intense, irresistible urge to go downstairs, open the door, go out to the lodge and beat Smerdyakov. Asked why, he could have given no exact reason, except perhaps that he loathed the valet as the man who had insulted him more seriously than anyone in the world. At other times that night he was overcome, more than once, by a sort of inexplicable, humiliating terror, which he felt was simply paralyzing his strength. His head ached and he was dizzy. A feeling of hatred rankled in his heart, as if he meant to take revenge on someone. He even hated Alyosha, remembering the talk he had just had with him. At moments he hated himself fiercely. He almost forgot to think about Katerina Ivanovna, and was greatly surprised at this afterwards, all the more because he remembered perfectly that when he had so valiantly declared to Katerina Ivanovna that he would leave for Moscow next day, something in his heart had whispered, “That’s nonsense, you’re not going, and tearing yourself away won’t be as easy as you’re boasting now.”

Years afterwards, remembering that night, Ivan recalled with peculiar disgust how he had suddenly got up from the sofa and, quietly, as if afraid someone would see him, opened the door, gone out on the staircase and listened to Fyodor Pavlovitch moving about below. He had listened for a long time—some five minutes—with a strange kind of curiosity, holding his breath, his heart pounding. Why he did all this, why he listened, he could not have said. All his life afterwards he called that “action” “infamous,” and deep in his heart he considered it the vilest action of his life. Toward Fyodor Pavlovitch himself he felt no hatred at that moment. He was simply intensely curious how the old man was walking about down there and what he might be doing. He wondered, and pictured him peeping out of the dark windows and halting in the middle of the room, listening, listening—for someone to knock. Ivan went out on the stairs to listen like this twice.

Around two o’clock, when all was quiet and even Fyodor Pavlovitch had gone to bed, Ivan lay down, firmly resolved to fall asleep at once, for he felt terribly exhausted. And fall asleep at once he did, and slept soundly without dreams, but woke early, at seven, in full daylight. Opening his eyes, he was surprised to find himself extraordinarily full of energy. He jumped up, dressed quickly, then hauled out his trunk and started packing straight away. His linen had come back from the laundress the morning before. Ivan actually smiled to think that everything was helping his sudden departure. And it was certainly sudden. The day before he had said (to Katerina Ivanovna, Alyosha and Smerdyakov) that he would leave next day. Yet he remembered that when he went to bed he had not been thinking of leaving at all, or at least had never dreamed that the first thing he would do in the morning was pack his trunk. At last his trunk and bag were ready. About nine o’clock Marfa Ignatyevna came in with her usual question, “Where will your honor take your tea, in your own room or downstairs?” He looked almost cheerful, but there was something hurried and scattered in him, in his words and gestures. He greeted his father warmly, even inquired particularly after his health, though he did not wait to hear the reply through. Then he announced that he was setting off in an hour to go back to Moscow for good, and asked him to send for the horses. His father took this news without any sign of surprise, and was ill-mannered enough to forget to show regret at losing him. Instead, he fell into a great flutter, remembering some important business of his own.

“What a fellow you are! Not telling me yesterday! Never mind, we’ll manage it all the same. Do me a big favor, my dear boy. Stop at Tchermashnya on your way. You just turn left at the Volovya station, another twelve versts and there’s Tchermashnya.”
“I’m sorry, I can’t. It’s eighty versts to the railway, and the Moscow train leaves at seven tonight. I’ll only just make it.”

“You’ll make it tomorrow or the day after. Today, turn off to Tchermashnya. Humoring your father won’t put you out much! If I weren’t tied up here, I’d have run over there myself long ago, because I have urgent business there. But here I ... this is no time for me to go.... You see, I own two pieces of woodland there. The Maslovs, an old merchant and his son, will give eight thousand for the timber. But last year I only just missed a buyer who’d have given twelve. You can’t get anyone around here to buy it. The Maslovs have everything their own way. You have to take what they offer, because no one here dares bid against them. Last Thursday the priest at Ilyinskoe wrote me that a merchant called Gorstkin, a man I know, had turned up. What makes him valuable is that he’s not from these parts, so he’s not afraid of the Maslovs. He says he’ll give me eleven thousand for the copse. Do you hear? But the priest writes that he’ll be here for a week only, so you must go at once and strike a bargain with him.”
“Well, write to the priest and he’ll strike it.”

“He can’t. He’s got no head for business. He’s an absolute treasure—I’d hand him twenty thousand to keep for me without a receipt—but he has no head for business. He’s a perfect child, a crow could fool him. And yet he’s a learned man, can you believe it? This Gorstkin looks like a peasant, he wears a blue kaftan, but he’s a regular rogue. That’s the common complaint. He’s a liar. Sometimes he lies so that you wonder why he bothers. The year before last he told me his wife was dead and he’d married another, and would you believe it, not a word of it was true? His wife never died at all, she’s alive today and thrashes him twice a week. So what you must find out is whether he’s lying or telling the truth when he says he wants to buy and would give eleven thousand.”
“I’d be no use in a business like that. I’ve no head for it either.”

“Hold on, wait! You will be of use, because I’ll tell you the signs by which you can size Gorstkin up. I’ve dealt with him for a long time. See, you have to watch his beard. He has a nasty, thin, red beard. If his beard shakes when he talks and he gets cross, that’s fine: he means what he says, he wants to do business. But if he strokes his beard with his left hand and grins, he’s trying to cheat you. Don’t watch his eyes, you’ll learn nothing from them, he’s a deep one, a rogue—watch the beard! I’ll give you a note and you show it to him. He’s called Gorstkin, though his real name is Lyagavy;[4] but don’t call him that, he’d be offended. If you come to terms with him and it looks all right, write me right away. All you need write is: ‘He’s not lying.’ Hold out for eleven thousand; you can knock off one thousand, but no more. Just think! There’s a world of difference between eight thousand and eleven. It’s as good as finding three thousand. Buyers aren’t easy to find, and I’m in desperate need of money. Just let me know it’s serious and I’ll run over and settle it. I’ll find the time somehow. But what’s the use of my galloping over there if it’s all just some idea of the priest’s? Well, will you go?”
